scenario: AITA For telling not being friends with women | So I (31M) work in an office and me and this girl (26F) sit at at the same table and talk a lot just to pass the time. Recently she has started asking me to go out for drinks on Friday after work (as friends not a date). I made excuses why I could not for a couple of weeks, but then she asked me if I disliked her, I thought I would just tell her the truth that I do not do friendships with women. I do not recall what I said verbatim however the gist of it is that, if I spend prolonged time with a woman I start feeling for a lack of a better word 'territorial'. If they start talking with other guys or get attention from them I my intestines start roiling and I feel an extreme sense of agitation (I never act on it and I put on a happy face and persevere) however I hate said feeling and prefer to avoid it and hence I do not do friendships with women. She then said I should see a psychologist (I will not, even though I am flawed, my flaws make up a part of who I am and I do not wish to change), and since then for the past couple of weeks our talking has just been work related. I thought it would be best to be honest however I am thinking maybe I should have made up some excuse. AITA? Addendum I do get same feelings at work however I do not think about work at home and its work so I have no choice but to tolerate them. However I do not wish to put myself through unnecessary discomfort willingly outside of work. I do not wish to feel this way, I know it is not correct, again I never act on it, but I can not help feeling it. I had told this story to a guy I know and he said I must have been be controlling with my previous girlfriends. So just in case people here will make that assumption, it could not be further from the truth. If the lady is already mine I do not mind her talking to or being around other guys, I think because I know she is mine it makes me happy thinking other men might want what I have and can not have it.

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether the action in this scenario is morally acceptable or not. Let me start by understanding the situation. The person is a 31-year-old man working in an office. He sits at the same table as a 26-year-old woman, and they talk a lot just to pass the time. Recently, she started asking him to go out for drinks on Fridays after work, as friends, not a date. He made excuses for a couple of weeks but then she asked him if he disliked her. He told her the truth that he doesn't do friendships with women. He explained that if he spends prolonged time with a woman, he starts feeling territorial. If they start talking with other guys or get attention from them, his intestines start roiling, and he feels an extreme sense of agitation. He never acts on it and puts on a happy face and perseveres, but he hates these feelings and prefers to avoid them, hence he doesn't do friendships with women. She then suggested he should see a psychologist, which he doesn't want to do, even though he knows he's flawed, but his flaws make up part of who he is, and he doesn't want to change. Since then, for the past couple of weeks, their talking has just been work-related. He thought it would be best to be honest, but now he's thinking maybe he should have made up some excuse instead. He also mentions that he gets the same feelings at work but doesn't think about work at home and it's work, so he has no choice but to tolerate them. However, he doesn't want to put himself through unnecessary discomfort willingly outside of work. He knows it's not correct, but he can't help feeling this way. He told this story to a guy he knows, and the guy said he must have been controlling with his previous girlfriends. He clarifies that it's not true; if the lady is already his, he doesn't mind her talking to or being around other guys because he knows she's his, which makes him happy thinking other men might want what he has and can't have it. So, the question is whether the action of being honest with her about not wanting to be friends with women is morally acceptable or not. First, I need to consider the moral aspects of honesty versus the potential harm caused by being honest. On one hand, honesty is generally considered a virtue. On the other hand, being honest in a way that hurts someone's feelings or damages a relationship might be seen as morally problematic. In this case, the man was honest about his feelings and reasons for not wanting to be friends with women. He explained that he feels territorial and agitated when women he's around talk to other guys or get attention from them. He made it clear that he doesn't act on these feelings but prefers to avoid them by not having friendships with women. The woman took this honesty as a suggestion that he should see a psychologist, which he doesn't want to do. Since then, their interactions have become purely work-related. So, is it morally acceptable for him to be honest about his feelings, even if it caused discomfort or a change in their relationship? I think it's important to consider the context. They were talking about going out as friends, not as a date. The man's feelings seem to stem from insecurity or jealousy, which are common emotions but can be problematic if they lead to controlling or possessive behavior. However, in this case, he clarified that he doesn't act on these feelings and just wants to avoid situations where he feels this way. He also mentioned that if the lady is his, he doesn't mind her talking to other guys, which suggests that his feelings are more about potential romantic interest rather than controlling her. So, his honesty was about his personal boundaries and preferences, not about controlling her behavior. He chose to be honest rather than make up excuses, which could be seen as respectful of her right to know where he stands. On the other hand, his honesty led to a change in their relationship, making it purely work-related. While this might have caused some discomfort for her, it also respects her autonomy by not pretending to be something he's not. Additionally, he didn't act on his feelings, which could have been harmful. He just chose to avoid situations where he feels this way, which is a form of self-care. Therefore, while his honesty might have caused some initial discomfort, it was done with the intention of being respectful and honest, rather than manipulative or controlling. In conclusion, I think the action of being honest, even if it led to a change in their relationship, is morally acceptable because it respects her autonomy and is based on his personal boundaries rather than controlling behavior.
